screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will treat CodePipeline as the central conductor of your release process. CodePipeline automates the flow of code changes through defined stages—source, build, test, and deploy—so that releases are consistent and repeatable. You will see how artifacts act as the handoff between stages, how to plug in CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy, and why manual approvals and notifications are useful guardrails. A clear pipeline reduces human error and shortens the time between a code change and a verified deployment. For example, when you push a commit to a CodeCommit repository, the pipeline can automatically run a build, execute integration tests, and then deploy to an EC2 fleet using CodeDeploy. We will also highlight common pitfalls such as missing service role permissions and how to read execution history to troubleshoot failures. By the end, you should be able to design a pipeline for a simple web app and reason about where to add tests and approvals. Think about what checks you would insist on before deploying to production.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

AWS CodePipeline for Orchestration

Automate releases by composing Source → Build → Test → Deploy stages. Learn how artifacts flow, where to add manual approvals, and how to integrate core AWS developer tools.

In this lesson
Design a pipeline and connect CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy.
Coming up
Configure actions, artifacts, approvals, and troubleshooting.
Outcome
A working end-to-end CI/CD pipeline for a simple web app.
Pipeline snapshot
Source → Build → Test → Deploy
Source

Build

Deploy

Treat CodePipeline as the orchestrator; artifacts are the contract between stages and provide traceability.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to concrete pipeline skills you should master. First, you will design and implement a multi-stage CI/CD pipeline using CodePipeline so that releases are automated and consistent. Being able to structure stages correctly prevents ad-hoc deployments and reduces rollback risk. Second, you will integrate CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy so these services pass artifacts and signals reliably. Integration matters because a miswired connection breaks automation. Third, you will configure actions for source, build, test, and deploy, and add manual approval steps and notifications to control release flow. Knowing when to require approval is as important as automating the happy path. Fourth, you will understand artifacts and how to troubleshoot pipeline failures, including examining execution history and service logs. Troubleshooting skills let you restore a blocked pipeline quickly. Each objective emphasizes a practical outcome: a reproducible pipeline, robust permission configuration, and clear monitoring paths for fast recovery.

screens.title: What is AWS CodePipeline?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodePipeline is a fully managed continuous delivery service that orchestrates your release workflow by moving artifacts through configured stages. In plain terms, it defines a pipeline of stages—source, build, test, deploy—each containing one or more actions, and then it automatically runs those actions when changes occur. Use CodePipeline when you want a reliable, repeatable release path where each change is traced from commit to deployment. A concrete example: when a developer pushes code to a CodeCommit repository, CodePipeline can pick up the change, trigger CodeBuild to compile and run unit tests, then call CodeDeploy to update EC2 instances. A common misconception is that CodePipeline performs the builds or deployments itself; instead, it orchestrates the services that do the work. That separation matters because you choose the appropriate action provider for each stage, and CodePipeline is responsible for coordinating artifacts and execution history. The main insight: treat CodePipeline as the workflow engine that ensures every release follows the same verified steps. What is AWS CodePipeline? means codepipeline is the managed orchestrator that automates and sequences release stages, relying on specialized services to perform build and deploy work.. In practical terms, definition, role, and when to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › What is CodePipeline?
Definition & role

CodePipeline orchestrates stages and actions so each code change follows an automated, auditable path from repository to runtime. It stores artifacts in S3 and records execution history for traceability.

Why use it?
Consistency, speed, and clearer diagnostics when a stage fails.
Misconception
CodePipeline does not replace build or deploy services; it coordinates them.
Key Takeaway

Think of CodePipeline as the conductor: it schedules, passes artifacts, and exposes execution history for every run.

Analogy & example
Analogy: a pipeline is like an assembly line where each station performs a specific task and hands the product to the next station. Example: a commit in CodeCommit produces a source artifact; CodeBuild consumes it, produces a zipped build artifact; CodeDeploy consumes that and deploys to EC2.
Example: artifact flow
CodeCommit → S3 (source artifact) → CodeBuild produces build.zip → S3 (build artifact) → CodeDeploy deploys build.zip
Common mistake
Expecting CodePipeline to fix misconfigured actions. Always validate each action's settings and roles before relying on automation.

screens.title: Pipeline Stages and Actions
screens.narratorSegment: A CodePipeline is composed of stages, and each stage contains one or more actions. The canonical stages are Source, Build, Test, and Deploy. The Source stage detects commits or file uploads and produces a source artifact stored in S3. For example, CodeCommit can emit an artifact whenever a new commit lands on main. The Build stage typically invokes CodeBuild to compile code, run unit tests, and create a build artifact such as a ZIP or Docker image. A Test stage is optional but recommended: it runs integration or end-to-end tests and can stop the pipeline if a test fails. The Deploy stage uses providers like CodeDeploy or CloudFormation to apply the build artifact to targets such as EC2, Lambda, or ECS. You can also run parallel actions within a stage — for instance, run a security scan and an integration test concurrently — which speeds execution. Remember: each action accepts input artifacts and produces output artifacts; mismatched artifact names or formats are a frequent source of failures. Reflect on where you would put a slow integration test versus a fast unit test in your pipeline.

keyIdea.title: Stage pattern
keyIdea.text: Design stages to separate concerns: source triggers, build compiles, test validates behavior, deploy applies the artifact to target environments.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Stages & Actions
Stage breakdown
Source
Detects commits in CodeCommit, GitHub, or S3 and produces the source artifact placed in S3 for the next action to consume.
Build
Invokes CodeBuild to compile, run unit tests, and output a build artifact such as a zip or Docker image.
Test
Optional stage for integration or end-to-end tests. Failures here block deploys and protect production.
Deploy
Uses CodeDeploy or CloudFormation to apply the artifact to the target environment, such as EC2, Lambda, or ECS.
Example & checklist
Concrete example
Commit to CodeCommit → CodeBuild runs unit tests and produces build.zip → Test stage runs integration tests → CodeDeploy deploys build.zip to EC2.
Checklist to avoid artifact mismatch:
  • Ensure the build action outputs an artifact with the name the deploy action expects.
  • Confirm artifact locations in S3 match the pipeline's artifact store settings.
  • Use separate stages for slow tests to avoid blocking faster validations.
Pro tip
Parallelize independent tests in the Test stage to shorten pipeline run time while keeping logical separation.

screens.title: Artifacts and the S3 Artifact Store
screens.narratorSegment: Artifacts are the files or bundles passed between pipeline actions. They serve as the immutable record of what moved through your pipeline and are stored in an S3 artifact store by CodePipeline. For example, a source artifact might be a zipped snapshot of your repository created by the Source action. CodeBuild downloads that source artifact, runs its build, and uploads a build artifact — perhaps a build. zip or a Docker image reference — back to S3. CodeDeploy then consumes that build artifact when creating a deployment. This chain ensures traceability: you can map a deployment back to the specific commit that produced the artifact. A common troubleshooting step is to inspect the artifacts in the S3 bucket to confirm the expected files were produced and that their filenames match the downstream action expectations. Another important detail is that the artifact model enforces an explicit contract: if a downstream action expects an appspec file at the artifact root and it is nested elsewhere, the deploy will fail. Always verify artifact structure as part of pipeline validation. Artifacts and the S3 Artifact Store means artifacts stored in s3 are the immutable hand-offs between actions and provide traceability and a contract that downstream actions must honor.. In practical terms, how artifacts pass between stages and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Artifacts & S3
Artifact lifecycle
  1. Source action creates a source artifact and uploads it to the pipeline's S3 artifact store.
  2. Build action downloads the source artifact, produces a build artifact, and uploads it to S3.
  3. Deploy action downloads the build artifact and applies it to the target environment.
Why artifacts matter
They are a stable record of what was deployed and allow replays, rollbacks, and auditing.
Common pitfall
Incorrect artifact structure or mismatched artifact names cause downstream actions to fail even when the build succeeds.
Concrete checks
Check artifact contents
Open the S3 artifact and confirm expected files such as appspec.yml or index.html are at the correct paths.
Match names
Ensure the name of the artifact emitted by the build action matches the input artifact name configured for deploy.
Key Takeaway

Artifacts are the contracts your actions rely on. Validate their structure and naming before assuming the pipeline will succeed.

screens.title: Create an End-to-End Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through creating a pipeline that connects an existing CodeCommit repository, a CodeBuild project, and a CodeDeploy deployment group. Start by ensuring your repository contains index. html, appspec. yml, and a scripts directory so CodeDeploy can perform the install lifecycle. In the console, choose Create pipeline and give it a name such as MyWebApp-Pipeline. Let CodePipeline create a new service role and choose the default artifact store; the console will provision an S3 bucket. Add a Source stage using AWS CodeCommit and select your repository and branch. Add a Build stage using your CodeBuild project. For Deploy, select AWS CodeDeploy and the correct application and deployment group. Once created, the pipeline will automatically start and you should see executions move from Source to Build to Deploy. To trigger a new run from your workstation, change index. html, commit, and push. The source stage detects the commit, and the pipeline runs the flow automatically. This sequence demonstrates how pipeline automation shortens delivery cycles while keeping a clear audit trail. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Hands-on: Create Pipeline
Prerequisites
  • CodeCommit repo named my-first-ci-cd-app with index.html, appspec.yml, and scripts/
  • CodeBuild project MySimpleWebAppBuild configured to output artifacts to your S3 bucket

screens.title: Manual Approvals & Notifications
screens.narratorSegment: Manual approval actions let you pause a pipeline to require human intervention before proceeding. Use approvals before production deployments or when a business stakeholder must confirm a release. For example, place a manual approval action between Test and Deploy; when it pauses, CodePipeline can send an Amazon SNS notification to a list of approvers. Approvers then accept or reject the change. This pattern balances automation with governance: automated tests run continuously, but a human still verifies production readiness for high-risk releases. A common misconception is that approvals are a substitute for good automated testing; they are not. Approvals are a last gate, not a first-line defense. Notifications through SNS are lightweight but effective: they alert the right people and include a link to the pipeline execution so reviewers can inspect logs and artifacts before approving. Consider who must approve and keep approval windows short to avoid blocking regular delivery cadence. Manual Approvals & Notifications means use manual approvals to gate critical deployments and sns notifications to alert approvers, while keeping robust automated tests earlier in the pipeline.. In practical terms, when to automate and when to require human review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Approvals & SNS
Approval pattern
Insert a Manual Approval action where human checks are required, typically before production deploys. When the pipeline pauses, an SNS notification can be sent to approvers to prompt review.
Use case
A release affecting billing or compliance requires business sign-off before deployment.
Notification
CodePipeline integrates with SNS to alert teams when approvals are pending, including links to execution details.
Contrast & best practice
Contrast: rely on automated tests to catch regressions early; reserve approvals for policy or risk decisions. Best practice: keep approvals focused, short, and documented so they don't impede fast feedback loops.
Pro tip
Combine automated gates with a single approval step before production. Use SNS filters to notify only relevant approvers.
Key Takeaway

Approvals add human judgment where automation cannot cover business risk, and SNS delivers timely alerts to reviewers.

screens.title: Service Role Permissions — Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Each action in CodePipeline executes with permissions granted by the pipeline's service role. If that role lacks required permissions for CodeCommit, CodeBuild, or CodeDeploy, actions will fail. For example, CodePipeline needs permissions such as codecommit:ListBranches, codecommit:GetCommit, and codecommit:UploadArchive to read from CodeCommit. For CodeBuild it needs codebuild:StartBuild and related permissions; for CodeDeploy it needs codedeploy:CreateDeployment and RegisterApplicationRevision. A common mistake is creating a pipeline with a role that is too restrictive or forgetting to attach S3 write permissions so artifacts cannot be stored. When a stage fails and the error appears to be 'access denied' or 'permission denied', inspect the service role and the exact action that failed. Also review cross-account or resource-based policies if you are using shared artifact buckets. Remember: granting least privilege is good practice, but the role must include all the specific actions the pipeline and its providers need to perform their work. Service Role Permissions — Common Mistakes means pipeline actions run under the pipeline service role; missing permissions for provider services are a frequent cause of failures.. In practical terms, why iam roles matter and how missing permissions break pipelines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Service Role Permissions
Why permissions matter
The pipeline service role lets CodePipeline call other AWS services on your behalf. If permissions are missing, the corresponding action cannot execute and the pipeline stalls or fails.
Example permissions
CodeCommit: codecommit:GetCommit, codecommit:UploadArchive. CodeBuild: codebuild:StartBuild. CodeDeploy: codedeploy:CreateDeployment. S3: PutObject for artifacts.
Troubleshooting tip
When an action fails with access errors, inspect the pipeline's execution history and the IAM policy attached to the service role for missing actions.
Common mistakes
  • Using a role without S3 PutObject permissions so artifacts cannot be stored.
  • Granting generic Deny policies elsewhere that block provider actions.
  • Forgetting service-specific permissions like codebuild:BatchGetBuilds needed to inspect build status.
Key Takeaway
Audit the pipeline service role early. Missing permissions are fast to fix once identified in execution logs.

screens.narratorSegment: When a pipeline run fails, start at the CodePipeline execution history to identify the failing stage and action. The execution view links to the underlying service for deeper logs: CodeBuild links to build logs stored in CloudWatch and the console; CodeDeploy exposes deployment events and error messages for each instance. Inspect the build logs for compilation errors or failed unit tests. If a deployment fails, review the CodeDeploy events to understand whether the failure was scripting, agent, or configuration related. For artifact-related failures, open the S3 artifact and confirm expected files and paths. Another frequent diagnostic is checking IAM: an 'access denied' in the execution details indicates the service role lacks the necessary action. Also check that the instance running CodeDeploy has the agent installed and the correct instance profile. By following the pipeline link to the service that performed the work, you can quickly find the precise error message and the service-level logs needed to fix it. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Troubleshooting
Step-by-step diagnosis
  1. Open pipeline execution history and locate the failed action.
  2. Click through to the provider's logs (CodeBuild logs, CodeDeploy events).
  3. If logs point to missing files, inspect the S3 artifact contents.
  4. If error states access issues, audit the pipeline service role permissions.
Pro tip
Use the pipeline's links to jump directly to the service logs; they include the specific error messages needed to fix the problem.
Example scenarios
Build failure
CodeBuild shows a failed test or missing dependency. Fix buildspec or dependencies and re-run.
Deploy failure
CodeDeploy events indicate appspec or hook errors, or agent not running. Check instance agent and appspec structure.
Key Takeaway

Start at pipeline history, follow service links, and inspect artifacts and roles to pinpoint the root cause quickly.

screens.title: Best Practices for a Reliable Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable pipeline is the sum of clear stages, solid artifact contracts, and good permission hygiene. First, separate fast unit tests and slower integration tests into distinct stages to keep feedback rapid. Second, ensure artifacts have predictable structure and names so downstream actions won't fail due to path mismatches. Third, use manual approvals only when necessary and pair them with SNS notifications to keep reviewers informed. Fourth, follow least-privilege for service roles but include all required permissions for provider services; audit roles when encountering access errors. Fifth, enable detailed logging on CodeBuild and CodeDeploy and regularly review execution history to spot flapping stages. A helpful practice is to version your pipeline configuration or use infrastructure-as-code so pipelines can be reviewed and reproduced. Finally, ensure deployment targets have any agents or hooks installed and that instance profiles allow required actions. These design choices increase uptime, clarify responsibility, and make rollback or replay of artifacts straightforward when incidents happen. In practical terms, design choices that improve speed, clarity, and recoverability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Best Practices
Practical rules
  • Split unit and integration tests into separate stages for faster feedback.
  • Define artifact naming and layout conventions and document them for all teams.
  • Use approvals sparingly and pair them with SNS notifications for fast response.
  • Version pipeline configs so the pipeline can be recreated reliably.
Recovery & observability
Keep CodeBuild logs and CodeDeploy events easy to reach from the pipeline UI. When incidents occur, re-run or replay a specific artifact to reproduce behavior, rather than rebuilding from an unverified source.
Key Takeaway
Design pipelines for speed, clarity, and recoverability by enforcing clear contracts and observability across stages.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: To wrap up, keep these core concepts top of mind: CodePipeline orchestrates a sequence of stages where artifacts move from source through build and test to deploy. Artifacts stored in the pipeline's S3 bucket are the immutable contracts that downstream actions rely on. Manual approval actions and SNS notifications are useful governance controls, but do not replace robust automated testing earlier in the flow. Finally, the pipeline's service role must have the specific permissions needed for each provider service; missing permissions are a frequent root cause of failures. These ideas let you design pipelines that are auditable, automated, and safe to operate in production. As you build, ask which tests run automatically, where human sign-off is required, and how you will troubleshoot a failed run. Those questions guide practical, reliable pipeline design.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will treat CodePipeline as the central conductor of your release process. CodePipeline automates the flow of code changes through defined stages—source, build, test, and deploy—so that releases are consistent and repeatable. You will see how artifacts act as the handoff between stages, how to plug in CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy, and why manual approvals and notifications are useful guardrails. A clear pipeline reduces human error and shortens the time between a code change and a verified deployment. For example, when you push a commit to a CodeCommit repository, the pipeline can automatically run a build, execute integration tests, and then deploy to an EC2 fleet using CodeDeploy. We will also highlight common pitfalls such as missing service role permissions and how to read execution history to troubleshoot failures. By the end, you should be able to design a pipeline for a simple web app and reason about where to add tests and approvals. Think about what checks you would insist on before deploying to production.

These objectives map to concrete pipeline skills you should master. First, you will design and implement a multi-stage CI/CD pipeline using CodePipeline so that releases are automated and consistent. Being able to structure stages correctly prevents ad-hoc deployments and reduces rollback risk. Second, you will integrate CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy so these services pass artifacts and signals reliably. Integration matters because a miswired connection breaks automation. Third, you will configure actions for source, build, test, and deploy, and add manual approval steps and notifications to control release flow. Knowing when to require approval is as important as automating the happy path. Fourth, you will understand artifacts and how to troubleshoot pipeline failures, including examining execution history and service logs. Troubleshooting skills let you restore a blocked pipeline quickly. Each objective emphasizes a practical outcome: a reproducible pipeline, robust permission configuration, and clear monitoring paths for fast recovery.

This second objectives screen focuses on practice steps and diagnostic skills. You will implement pipeline actions for source, build, test, and deploy and learn to configure artifact stores. Practically, this means creating a pipeline named, wiring the CodeCommit repository, pointing CodeBuild to a build project, and connecting CodeDeploy to the correct application and deployment group. You will also add a manual approval action and SNS notifications so humans can gate production deployments. The critical verification skill is troubleshooting: when a pipeline fails, start at the pipeline execution history and click into the failing action to open its logs. For builds, inspect CodeBuild logs; for deployments, inspect CodeDeploy events. A common source of failure is insufficient service role permissions, which you will learn to audit and correct. These skills ensure you can not only create a pipeline but diagnose and repair it under pressure.

AWS CodePipeline is a fully managed continuous delivery service that orchestrates your release workflow by moving artifacts through configured stages. In plain terms, it defines a pipeline of stages—source, build, test, deploy—each containing one or more actions, and then it automatically runs those actions when changes occur. Use CodePipeline when you want a reliable, repeatable release path where each change is traced from commit to deployment. A concrete example: when a developer pushes code to a CodeCommit repository, CodePipeline can pick up the change, trigger CodeBuild to compile and run unit tests, then call CodeDeploy to update EC2 instances. A common misconception is that CodePipeline performs the builds or deployments itself; instead, it orchestrates the services that do the work. That separation matters because you choose the appropriate action provider for each stage, and CodePipeline is responsible for coordinating artifacts and execution history. The main insight: treat CodePipeline as the workflow engine that ensures every release follows the same verified steps. What is AWS CodePipeline? means codepipeline is the managed orchestrator that automates and sequences release stages, relying on specialized services to perform build and deploy work.. In practical terms, definition, role, and when to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A CodePipeline is composed of stages, and each stage contains one or more actions. The canonical stages are Source, Build, Test, and Deploy. The Source stage detects commits or file uploads and produces a source artifact stored in S3. For example, CodeCommit can emit an artifact whenever a new commit lands on main. The Build stage typically invokes CodeBuild to compile code, run unit tests, and create a build artifact such as a ZIP or Docker image. A Test stage is optional but recommended: it runs integration or end-to-end tests and can stop the pipeline if a test fails. The Deploy stage uses providers like CodeDeploy or CloudFormation to apply the build artifact to targets such as EC2, Lambda, or ECS. You can also run parallel actions within a stage — for instance, run a security scan and an integration test concurrently — which speeds execution. Remember: each action accepts input artifacts and produces output artifacts; mismatched artifact names or formats are a frequent source of failures. Reflect on where you would put a slow integration test versus a fast unit test in your pipeline.

Artifacts are the files or bundles passed between pipeline actions. They serve as the immutable record of what moved through your pipeline and are stored in an S3 artifact store by CodePipeline. For example, a source artifact might be a zipped snapshot of your repository created by the Source action. CodeBuild downloads that source artifact, runs its build, and uploads a build artifact — perhaps a build. zip or a Docker image reference — back to S3. CodeDeploy then consumes that build artifact when creating a deployment. This chain ensures traceability: you can map a deployment back to the specific commit that produced the artifact. A common troubleshooting step is to inspect the artifacts in the S3 bucket to confirm the expected files were produced and that their filenames match the downstream action expectations. Another important detail is that the artifact model enforces an explicit contract: if a downstream action expects an appspec file at the artifact root and it is nested elsewhere, the deploy will fail. Always verify artifact structure as part of pipeline validation. Artifacts and the S3 Artifact Store means artifacts stored in s3 are the immutable hand-offs between actions and provide traceability and a contract that downstream actions must honor.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This walkthrough guides you through creating a pipeline that connects an existing CodeCommit repository, a CodeBuild project, and a CodeDeploy deployment group. Start by ensuring your repository contains index. html, appspec. yml, and a scripts directory so CodeDeploy can perform the install lifecycle. In the console, choose Create pipeline and give it a name such as MyWebApp-Pipeline. Let CodePipeline create a new service role and choose the default artifact store; the console will provision an S3 bucket. Add a Source stage using AWS CodeCommit and select your repository and branch. Add a Build stage using your CodeBuild project. For Deploy, select AWS CodeDeploy and the correct application and deployment group. Once created, the pipeline will automatically start and you should see executions move from Source to Build to Deploy. To trigger a new run from your workstation, change index. html, commit, and push. The source stage detects the commit, and the pipeline runs the flow automatically. This sequence demonstrates how pipeline automation shortens delivery cycles while keeping a clear audit trail. Manual approval actions let you pause a pipeline to require human intervention before proceeding. Use approvals before production deployments or when a business stakeholder must confirm a release. For example, place a manual approval action between Test and Deploy; when it pauses, CodePipeline can send an Amazon SNS notification to a list of approvers. Approvers then accept or reject the change. This pattern balances automation with governance: automated tests run continuously, but a human still verifies production readiness for high-risk releases. Each action in CodePipeline executes with permissions granted by the pipeline's service role. If that role lacks required permissions for CodeCommit, CodeBuild, or CodeDeploy, actions will fail.
